facts: This is an appeal u/s.2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, against the judgment dated 10th October, 1977, of the High Court of Kerala, setting aside the acquittal of the two appellants of offences u/s.341 and 302 read with S.34 of the Indian Penal Code recorded by the First Additional Sessions Judge, Trivandrum and convicting them of an offence u/s.302 aforesaid, with finding that it was committed in furtherance of the common intention of them both
The two appellants harboured feelings of animosity against the deceased Janardhana Kurup, who was irrigating his field at 8.30 p.m. on 8th December, 1975.
The occurrence was witnessed by Kuttan Pillai (P.W.1) and Vijayan (P.W.2) who is a son of the deceased.

After Janardhana Kurup was taken home, he was removed to the hospital attached to the Medical College at Trivandrum where he told Dr. Sivaprasad (P.W.10) that 'Sree Kumar stabbed while at the door of the house with some weapon'.
The two appellants absconded after the occurrence and were not traceable for a month

The evidence relied on by the prosecution mainly consisted of the ocular version of the occurrence given by Kuttan Pillai (P.W.1) and Vijayan (P.W.2), the corroboration of the testimony of the former by the contents of first information report Ex-P.1, the dying declaration made by the deceased to Dr. Sivaprasad (P.W.10), the medical evidence and the circumstance that the accused were not available to the Police for more than a month after the occurrence
The chief reasons recorded by the learned Sessions Judge for acquitting the two appellants may be summarised thus
It is undisputed that some bad blood existed between the deceased on the one hand and the appellants on the other prior to the occurrence.
There is no doubt about the place where Janardhana Kurup was stabbed and the same is situated at a short distance from his house as well as that of Kuttan Pillai (P.W.1).
The first information report in our opinion, is not a document attended with any unavoidable delay.
The deceased was rushed to the hospital at Trivandrum with all possible speed and had been examined by the doctor within two hours of the occurrence.
issues: Whether the acquittal of the appellants was proper
Whether the prosecution evidence is reliable
petitioner_arguments: The learned Sessions Judge for acquitting the two appellants may be summarised thus

The chief reasons recorded by the learned Sessions Judge for acquitting the two appellants are either flimsy or ill-founded and were not at all sufficient to discard the testimony of the eye-witnesses or the dying declaration, both of which pieces of evidence were found to be otherwise reliable, supported as they were by the medical evidence
respondent_arguments: The prosecution case may be stated thus
The main thing to be seen is whether those inconsistencies, etc. go to the root of the matter or pertain to insignificant aspects thereof.
court_reasoning: We are of the opinion that the judgment of the High Court is unexceptionable and that the grounds on which the trial Court ordered the acquittal of the appellants are either non-existent or too trivial to merit attention.
The variation in human nature being so vast, murders are known to have been actuated by much lesser motives.
So long as the other evidence remains convincing and is not open to reasonable doubt, a conviction may well be based on it
The first information report was made next morning to the police when it arrived at the hospital while the deceased was still alive but fighting a losing battle.
Vijayan (P.W.2) and his friends must have been under shock for quite some time after the occurrence and then, as already stated, their chief concern must have been to save the life of the victim.
holding: The appeal before us accordingly fails and is dismissed
